title: Commercial Renovation Planning in Winnipeg: A Business Guide
metaTitle: Commercial Renovation Planning in Winnipeg | Bridgeland
metaDescription: Plan a commercial renovation in Winnipeg without losing customers: timeline stages, phasing, after-hours work, staff and customer notices, and occupancy.
excerpt: How to plan a major renovation around a business that needs to keep running: the stages from site visit to occupancy permit, keeping customers informed, and a checklist to start with.
answer: Start from the date you need the space back and work backwards: written scope and quote, drawings, permits, construction in phases or after hours, inspections and the occupancy permit. Tell staff and customers early, keep accessible routes open or announce when they are not, and plan restocking, training and reopening for after the City allows occupancy.

faqs.q: How do I keep my business open while renovating?
faqs.a: Phase the work so part of the space stays open, schedule noisy or disruptive tasks for evenings and weekends within the City's noise hours, and separate work areas from customers. Tell customers early which entrance and services are available. Bridgeland Builders offers after-hours and weekend scheduling for commercial work and sends a progress update every week.

Write down why you are renovating, what must stay open and when you need the space back, then book an on-site visit before committing to a design or lease change. That visit shows what the building allows and which approvals apply, and it leads to a written quote you can plan and finance around.

faqs.q: What commonly delays a commercial renovation?
faqs.a: Late design changes, plan review comments that take time to answer, hidden conditions such as asbestos or old wiring, long-lead equipment, and inspections that are not requested in time. Many of these shrink when the design is finished and the building investigated before work starts, and when each inspection is requested as soon as its stage is ready.

faqs.q: Do I have to close if our accessible entrance is affected?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but you must tell people. Manitoba's Accessible Customer Service Standard requires organizations with at least one employee to let the public know when and why an accessibility feature is unavailable. Where you can, offer an alternative accessible route or way to get service, and post the notice at the entrance and online.

faqs.q: How do I choose the right contractor for a business renovation?
faqs.a: Look for commercial experience similar to your project, a clear written quote, a realistic schedule and a plan for working around your hours. Ask how permits, inspections and progress updates are handled. Our guide on [how to choose a renovation contractor](/blog/how-to-choose-the-right-contractor-for-your-renovation-project) has a full checklist of questions.

blocks.x: A major renovation tests a business twice: once in the construction, and again in keeping customers, staff and revenue intact while it happens. Businesses that come through well treat the renovation as a project with its own plan, not something that happens around them. This guide sets out the stages of a commercial renovation in Winnipeg, how to stay open through them, and what to settle before the first day of work.
What does a commercial renovation project timeline look like?

Most projects move through the same stages: site visit and scope, design and drawings, permits, ordering and investigation, construction with progress inspections, final inspections and the occupancy permit, then move-in and deficiency work. How long each stage takes depends on the scope and approvals, so ask for a schedule alongside your written quote.

blocks.x: How do you keep your business open during a renovation?

Phase the work so part of the space keeps operating, move disruptive tasks to evenings and weekends, and separate work areas from customers with temporary walls and controlled access. If a full closure is unavoidable, make it as short as possible by finishing design, approvals and ordering before the closure starts.

Two Winnipeg rules shape this. Within 150 metres of a home, the City allows loud construction work only from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends and holidays, so loud work cannot run overnight near homes. And the City's occupancy bulletin says the general contractor is responsible for the safety of everyone entering the construction site before the occupancy permit is issued, so keep customers and staff out of active work areas.

Bridgeland Builders schedules commercial work in the evenings and on weekends where it helps, and sends a progress update every week so you can plan staffing around the next phase. Clinics have extra constraints around patients and accessibility; see our [medical and dental office renovations](/services/medical-dental-office-renovations).
What should you tell staff and customers?

Tell them early and be specific: which areas close and when, how to get in, what hours change, and who to contact. Staff need the schedule, temporary work arrangements and safety rules. Customers need clear signs, website and social updates, and notice of any accessibility feature that will be out of use.

That last point is a requirement, not a courtesy. Manitoba's Accessible Customer Service Standard applies to every organization with at least one employee and includes letting the public know when and why an accessibility feature is unavailable. The Manitoba Accessibility Office publishes a notice of service disruption template you can adapt.
Update your hours on your website, social accounts and online listings before each phase.
Post signs showing the open entrance, the accessible route and any temporary service point.
Give staff a one-page schedule of what closes when, and who to call with site questions.
Plan your reopening message for after the occupancy permit, not before.
How should you budget for disruption?

Add the costs of operating through a renovation to the construction budget: sales lost during closures, temporary space or storage, overtime, moving and IT work, extra cleaning, and rent paid while you cannot trade. Then add a contingency. BDC advises setting aside a contingency fund and buffer time, because renovations often run over budget and past deadline.

Our guides to [the biggest cost factors in commercial renovation projects](/blog/the-biggest-cost-factors-in-commercial-renovation-projects) and [commercial renovation financing in Manitoba](/blog/how-to-finance-a-commercial-renovation-without-breaking-the-bank) go deeper on the construction budget and how to pay for it.
When can you move back in?

When the City has issued an interim or final building occupancy permit for the renovated area, where one is required. That needs progress inspections completed to the final stage, plus professional certifications if an architect or engineer was involved. Until then, the City counts stocking shelves, training staff, meeting clients and conducting business as occupying the space.

Construction and the delivery and installation of fixed equipment and furniture are allowed before the permit, but stock, supplies and personal belongings are not, so keep stock off-site and schedule computer and printer installation, staff training and any soft opening for after it. Outside Winnipeg, check the equivalent rules with your municipality's permit office.
Checklist before the first day of work
Confirm the lease allows the work, and get the landlord's consent and any building rules in writing.
Write down your goals, the dates that cannot move and the date you need the space back.
Book an on-site visit and get a written quote with the scope, exclusions and a proposed schedule.
List every approval: building and trade permits, a development permit if the use changes, and health, liquor or X-ray approvals where they apply.
In an older building, get the asbestos inventory before demolition is scheduled; where asbestos may be present, Manitoba requires one before work begins.
Agree the phasing plan and which work happens after hours.
Prepare staff and customer notices, including any accessibility disruption notice.
Set your reopening date after the expected occupancy permit, not before it.
